chapter_theme: Paripadal 21, to Sevvel at Parankunram: the god named by what he rides, wears, holds and dwells on, the hill's women in their sulks and adornments seen as a painting, the hill's creatures as an orchestra, a husband's plunge after his wife in a pool, and a wife's dance to her husband's drum before the prayer to dwell at his feet; and Paripadal 22, to the Vaiyai, broken by gaps: the rain told as the king's war and gifts, the procession to the bank, lovers who may be the river's ornament or it theirs, and the sounds of the Thirumarutham ford.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god by his mount, dress, weapon, garland and hill, a கடவுள் வாழ்த்து under paadaan (porul 2.27)

paripadal:21:1-17.reading: The poet names the god's possessions one by one, what he rides (a war elephant famed for battles won, a fire-bright frontlet flashing on its head), what he has put on (a garment of stitched hide and strips of soft peacock feather, worked like a striped snakeskin strap), what is in his hand (the spear that cut down the mango trunk of the unyielding foe and split open the hill named after a bird), what he wears (a fragrant garland of round kadamba clusters woven through with curling valli creeper) and what he has settled on (cool Parankunram, praised on the tongues of the worthy, girdled at its waist by seven rows of long-leaved paalai trees, with pools of sweet water, a hill that earth and sky delight in), and prays, worshipping the victor with the banner, that dwelling at the foot of that hill be granted.
paripadal:21:1-17.nuance: The unit is a catechism: five neuter nouns (ஊர்ந்ததை, தொட்டதை, கையதை, பூண்டதை, அமர்ந்ததை, 'what he rode, touched, held, wore, settled on') each answered in turn, and the last answer is a place, so the hill is counted among the god's belongings like his spear and garland. The prayer asks for nothing but residence: குன்றத்து அடி, the foot of the hill, also reads as the god's feet. Lines 3 to 7, the garment, are compressed and their syntax is a reading.

comparisons.tenor: the gold frontlet on the elephant's brow
the strips of the god's garment
the rows of paalai trees round the hill's middle

thinai_evidence.note: a woman sulking at her husband, marutham's uri, set on the kurinji hill of the god

paripadal:21:18-29.reading: On the god's hill one woman, dancing with anklets of gold whose pearl pellets ring as she steps to the drum and swings her arms, held back by the joy of brewed toddy, turns eyes red as a bright spear point on the husband who would embrace her and sulks; another looks into a mirror to see her reflection and sets right her fire-bright jewels; another smears sandal between her swelling breasts, rubs it off, and wants it applied again; thought over and over, says the poet to the god who cut down the mango, these scenes are like the beauty a master paints in a picture.
paripadal:21:18-29.nuance: The three women are given as states (நிலையும், குறிப்பும், விருப்பும்: her stance, her intent, her desire), so the poet paints moods, not deeds, and calls the whole a painting; the sulk, the mirror and the sandal are the household's oodal and toilet carried up to the shrine hill. Line 26 (பின் உற ஊட்டுவாள்) is compressed, and who is to apply the sandal again is our reading; line 21 is a repaired line.

comparisons.tenor: the women's moods seen on the hill

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god's hill as a place where every creature sounds together, under paadaan

paripadal:21:30-38.reading: On the hill of the god with the resounding drum, everything sounds at once: the spotted peacock, spreading its tail on both sides like a fan raised overhead at the thunder of the cloud, dances; the humming thumbi blows into the opened flowers as a flute is blown through the holes the fingers close; the new-come swarms of bees bring forth the music of the lute; and the waterfall brims with the sound of the beating drum.
paripadal:21:30-38.nuance: No human player is named: the hill itself is the orchestra, peacock for dancer, thumbi for flute, bees for lute, falls for drum, and the only drum that is a drum is the god's own (இரங்கு முரசினான்), so the god is named by the one instrument the creatures answer. A line before line 30 may have been dropped as a heading (flag).

comparisons.tenor: the hum of the bee swarms

thinai_evidence.note: a husband's embrace of his wife in a pool on the hill: union, with the things of the kurinji hill

paripadal:21:39-53.reading: A woman in fine jewels who has bathed in the middle of a deep, echoing pool rises above the water; in the play, as a bowl of flower-water is flung, she has no float and is in distress in the deep water, and her husband, seeing it, giddy with joy, drops into the flower-strewn water and embraces her: such is cool Parankunram; and the god's hill, its falls spreading over steep clefts, has these winds in plenty, the wind mixed with the cool fragrant sandal that young men rubbed on, the wind that stirred the cloud-dark hair of fish-eyed women and shook out its scented dust, and the wind that passed through the fragrant smoke raised for the tall Vel of the kadamba.
paripadal:21:39-53.nuance: The three winds (வளியும் three times) carry the hill's three kinds of scent, men's sandal, women's hair, the god's incense, so lovers and worship are one air on the hill. The rescue in the pool turns a moment of danger into the embrace, the husband's joy (மகிழ் தூங்கி) coming before he plunges. Lines 40 to 42 are hard: who is told to let go of whom (கேள்வனை ... விடுக) and who throws the bowl is our reading.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife's dance to her husband's drum is held inside the closing praise and prayer, so the unit is paadaan

paripadal:21:54-70.reading: A woman whose chaplet, set at intervals with bright gold plates flashing like a creeper of lightning, falls along her hair, held back by honey liquor like a gem, sways, her green cloth loosening and her eyes reddening, bending like a flowering creeper to the beat of the drum her worthy husband rolls, her pearl chain swaying on her breasts, her cloth swaying, her ornaments swaying and she swaying like a branch ruffled by the north wind; her eyes as she shifts her shoulders to the drum are like rolling arrows; and the poet, hailing the god who wielded the fierce spear that won the battle, of twelve shoulders and six spread faces, prays with his glad company that their dwelling at the god's feet be granted as it is today, worshipping the lord who wore down his foes.
paripadal:21:54-70.nuance: The husband plays the drum and the wife dances, so a married pair performs the hill's rite together, and the prayer at the close asks that 'today' recur (இன்று போல் இயைக), the same refrain as line 16 with the hill's foot now the god's feet. Lines 66 and 67 may continue the woman's eyes (that drive the spear, as his do) or turn to the god in epithets; we read them as epithets.

comparisons.tenor: the gold plates in her chaplet
the woman swaying with cloth and ornaments
her eyes moving to the drum

thinai_evidence.note: the river's rain and flood praised through the king's war and gifts, under paadaan

paripadal:22:1-16.reading: Clouds press on like the rows of elephants that the shining-sworded lord of hills halted in the battle where bodies fell; thunder rolls like the drum of the one of unceasing wrath who overcame kings; the rain falls scattering swift drops like the arrows loosed by the bows of his army against the unyielding; lightning flashes fierce as his gleaming spear; and the water the sky poured like his bounty gathers on the earth without stopping and, like his army, enters all the land where it went, the fields full of sheaves; the rest of the passage, broken by gaps, speaks of hills and sand, a drum beaten, and the flood coming on head to head in strength.
paripadal:22:1-16.nuance: Every part of the storm is copied from the king: his elephants, drum, arrows, spear and, last, his giving, so the monsoon that makes the Vaiyai is told as the king's war and the king's bounty at once, and the flood that enters the fields is his army taking ground. Lines 10 and 12 to 15 have gaps, and line 13 is garbled.

thinai_evidence.note: the town's procession to the river for the festival bathing, praise of the river's day under paadaan

paripadal:22:17-25.reading: People come carrying red dye, incense and sandal paste, things fit for the wet-dress of the bathing, and many fine flowered cloths, with others following behind; women with red flower chaplets of close work and garlands of petals of fresh vetchi, men with garlands and crowns and handsome chests; and horses, elephants and gem-adorned mules crowd the bank and fill the groves.
paripadal:22:17-25.nuance: ஈரணி, the dress for wet play, names a festival kit: things are brought to be worn in the water. Line 17 is garbled after a dropped heading and line 20 has a gap, so the opening of the list is our reading.

thinai_evidence.note: lovers on the river bank, the women as the reward of the men's penance: union by the river

paripadal:22:26-35.reading: With young men in warrior anklets, strong as the god who wields the spear and lovely as the god of the fragrant flower arrows, come women counted the fruit of the garlanded men's penance, with hair dark as the rain cloud, carp eyes, lips like the kavir flower, long-banded breasts, girdles of fine work and bright teeth and smiles; those who try to judge ask whether these are an ornament to the famed Vaiyai or the Vaiyai's ornamented flood an ornament to them, and cannot decide: such is the beauty where the bank and the Vaiyai meet.
paripadal:22:26-35.nuance: The praise is a doubt that will not resolve (தேர்தற்கு அரிது): the river and the women each seem the other's ornament, so the festival beauty belongs to neither alone but to their meeting (தீரமும் வையையும் சேர்கின்ற). The men are given two gods for models at once, Murugan for strength and Kama for beauty.

comparisons.vehicle: வேல் ஆற்றும் பொய்ம்பனின், விரை மலர் அம்பினோன்

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the sounds at the river's sacred ford, under paadaan

paripadal:22:36-50.reading: To the sweet beat of the earth-clay drum something answers sound for sound (the line is broken), the lute of forked strings sounds, in the grove the spotted swarms of bees hum on the flowering branches, the sweet flute plays its measure, the thumbi sipping pollen on the flowers sounds without pause, and, as the hand drum keeps time, the wind, a dancer, makes the soft-clustered flowering creeper sway: so at the Thirumarutham ford of the sweet-watered Vaiyai all these take up each other's work; then, in broken lines, a woman is described, dark heavy hair swinging, long soft shoulders drooping like a creeper whose leaves and flowers do not wilt, a long trailing cloth and anklets striped with pearls.
paripadal:22:36-50.nuance: தத்தம் தொழில் மாறு கொள்ளும், 'they exchange their work', is the point: at the ford the town's instruments and the grove's creatures answer each other, the wind takes the dancer's part and the bees the singer's. Lines 37, 42, 47 and 50 are broken, and the woman of lines 46 to 50 cannot be fully read.

links.note: Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet (இறைவன் அடிசேரா தார்) cross the sea of births; Paripadal 21.16 asks only that dwelling at the foot of the god's hill (குன்றத்து அடி உறை) be granted, and line 68 repeats it as dwelling at the god's feet (நின் அடி உறை).
links.teaches: The Kural's feet are a way out of rebirth, while the Paripadal makes the same feet a place on the ground, the foot of one hill where worshippers ask to go on living, so the pair shows the god's feet as a refuge of release in the ethical book and as a home on earth in the older festival hymn.

links.note: Kural 1090 says brewed toddy (அடுநறா) delights only those who drink it, unlike love, which delights those who see it; Paripadal 21.20 has a dancer held by the joy of brewed toddy (அடு நறா மகிழ்) sulking at her husband, and the poet says such scenes, when recalled, are a painting's beauty.
links.teaches: The Kural separates the drinker's private pleasure from the beholder's pleasure in love, while the Paripadal mixes them in one woman, drunk and sulking at her husband, and makes her a picture for onlookers on the hill, so held together they show that at the shrine festival even the drinker's mood became something seen and enjoyed by others.

links.note: Akananuru 82.1-10 makes the hill country a stage: wind in bamboo the flute, the waterfall the drum, bees the lute, monkeys the audience and the peacock a dancer; Paripadal 21.30-38 has the peacock dance, the thumbi as flute, bees as lute and the waterfall as drum on the god's hill.
links.teaches: In the Akananuru the hill's orchestra is a love poem's setting, praising the hill man's country and ending in the woman's lonely night, while the Paripadal keeps the same instruments, drops the monkey audience and the lovers, and gives the scene to the god with the drum, so the pair shows a figure from akam landscape reused as worship of the hill's own god.

links.note: In Paripadal 6.88-92 a husband says a woman bathing in his pool, swept under by a wave, fell on him unbidden, and swears by cool Parankunram; in Paripadal 21.39-45 a wife at a pool on Parankunram loses her float and her husband plunges in and embraces her.
links.teaches: The Vaiyai song's husband uses a fall in the water as an alibi for touching another woman and swears by Parankunram, while the Parankunram song shows the water embrace on that hill as a husband's rescue of his own wife, so the pair shows one festival accident read either as an excuse for straying or as wedded love.

links.note: Paripadal 5.79-81 says what we ask of the god is not wealth, gold or pleasure (பொருளும் பொன்னும் போகமும் அல்ல) but grace, love and aram; Paripadal 21.68-70, after the drinking and dancing of the hill, asks that dwelling at his feet be granted as today (இன்று போல்), with their company.
links.teaches: The two Murugan songs end in prayers to the same god that pull apart: one refuses pleasure and asks for inner gifts, the other asks that a festival day of liquor, dance and couples simply recur, so the anthology holds both a moral and a festive idea of what worship should obtain.

links.note: Purananuru 107 answers the poets who praise Pari alone: there is also the rain (மாரியும் உண்டு) that sustains the world; Paripadal 22.8 says the sky poured water like the king's bounty (அவன் வண்மைபோல் வானம் பொழிந்த நீர்), after likening clouds, thunder, drops and lightning to his elephants, drum, arrows and spear.
links.teaches: Kapilar measures the patron against the rain and lets the rain win, while the Paripadal measures the rain against the king and makes the whole storm a copy of his war and gifts, so held together they show the rain-and-giving comparison run in both directions, with the river hymn making the king the original and nature the likeness.

links.note: Paripadal 8.112-117 says the eyes, faces, feet, hands, breasts and lips of girls rising from the hill pool cannot be told apart from the lotus and lilies of the water; Paripadal 22.32-34 says onlookers cannot decide whether the women adorn the Vaiyai or the Vaiyai's flood adorns them.
links.teaches: The hill song confuses women and flowers part by part, while the river song lifts the doubt to the whole, women against river, and refuses to settle which is the ornament, so the pair shows the Paripadal using the undecided likeness as its stock praise of festival bathing and widening it from a catalogue to a single question.

links.note: Paripadal 21.30-38 makes the peacock, thumbi, bees and waterfall into dancer, flute, lute and drum on the god's hill; Paripadal 22.36-44 has real drum, lute, flute and hand drum sounding with bees and thumbi at the Vaiyai ford, the wind as dancer (வளி நடன்), and says they exchange their work (தொழில் மாறு கொள்ளும்).
links.teaches: On the hill the orchestra is made of creatures only, while at the river the town's instruments and the grove's creatures play together and trade parts, so the two songs, set side by side in one chapter, show the hill as nature performing for its god and the ford as the town and nature performing with each other.

source_issues: Paripadal 21 and 22: the colophons have no thinai or thurai; 21's pan is காந்தாரம, a musical mode, and 22 has no poet, music or pan (தெரியவில்லை).
Paripadal 21 line 30 and 22 line 17: a line was taken for a modern heading and dropped before them (flags); not checked by eye.
Paripadal 21 lines 9 and 21 and 22 line 7 are repaired from sangamtamil.com's reading (flags); 21 line 11 has ஒன்ணுபடு, likely a misprint.
Paripadal 22 lines 10, 12, 14, 15, 20, 37, 42, 47 and 50 have gaps; line 50 has no Tamil letters, and line 13 (கான மலைத்தரை கொன்று மணல பினறி) and line 17 (பொறிவி யாற்றுறி) are garbled.
Paripadal 22 lines 18, 19, 37, 38 and 39 are not in sangamtamil.com's text; the flag that line 1 differs strongly compares it with 21's line 63, so sangamtamil.com's alignment is off by a song there.
